\section{The Semantic Layer}
\label{sec:semantic}

Sections~\ref{sec:architecture}--\ref{sec:slb} describe a kernel that retrieves quickly. Retrieval speed, however, is not the binding constraint on long-horizon memory quality. We established this by constructing an \textbf{oracle}: an arm handed the gold answer-bearing turns directly, with nothing to retrieve. On LongMemEval-S the oracle answers only 419 of 500 questions. \textbf{Twenty-eight questions are wrong under the oracle, under extract-then-compute, and under single-shot alike} --- perfect evidence, wrong answer --- and they are dominated by counting and aggregation. The canonical case asks how many music albums the user has purchased; the gold answer is three, and an oracle holding all three mentions answers two, because counting scattered mentions is a multi-hop operation performed inside the reader.

This motivates a second memory layer that stores not what was said but what it \emph{means}.

\subsection{Consolidated Records}

At ingest time, each session is compressed --- \emph{query-blind}, since a real consolidator cannot see future questions --- into durable \textbf{records}, stored as Atlas nodes. A record carries a kind (\texttt{ITEM}, \texttt{FACT}, \texttt{EVENT}, \texttt{UPDATE}, \texttt{PREF}, \texttt{TASK}), a bucket drawn from a \textbf{closed twelve-category vocabulary}, a free-form subtype, an optional date, and a provenance link.

The closed vocabulary is load-bearing rather than stylistic. A free-form category field was implemented first and failed for a specific, reproducible reason: independent per-session extraction calls invent their own category names, so members of one real category scatter and never accumulate. Of three albums, one was recorded as an \texttt{ITEM}, one as a \texttt{PREF}, and one as an \texttt{EVENT}; enumerating \texttt{ITEM}s returned one against a gold of three. Under the closed taxonomy the same question answers three.

\subsection{Provenance as a Dual-Purpose Index}

Records are lossy by construction, and we measured what that costs. Compressing to bare facts destroys \emph{pragmatic licensing}: ``picked it up at Trader Joe's'' answers ``what brand?'' only by conversational implicature, and discarding the surrounding turn cost twelve questions when extract-then-compute did it. Retaining one conversational turn on each side of the evidence recovers it (63/64 on the affected type, against 55 without).

Every record therefore stores the session identifier and turn indices it derives from, and the read path rehydrates that neighbourhood on demand. Provenance is deliberately \emph{not} stored as raw node identifiers: an Atlas node id can shift after compaction reclaims tombstoned slots, whereas a session id plus a turn index survives it.

The same field turns out to be the \textbf{right-to-erasure cascade index}. Records are personally identifying information derived from conversation, and tombstoning an Atlas node does not by itself reach the records derived from it. Because every record names its source session, honouring a deletion request is a filter on provenance rather than a new mechanism.

\subsection{The Composite Read Path}

A query assembles one prompt from two \emph{different} information sources: the complete record set, plus a bounded budget of verbatim episodic turns rehydrated from those records' own provenance. This is a composite, not a router, and the distinction is empirical. Routing between the two arms was measured three separate times and never beat always-on inclusion; the type-label oracle ceiling sat at or inside the noise band every time. Those arms carried the \emph{same} information, so choosing between them could only lose. Records and raw turns do not: each answers questions the other cannot.

\textbf{All records are included, rather than a top-$k$ retrieval over them.} Vector retrieval over records would fetch three of five members of a category and reintroduce partial recall on exactly the counting questions this layer exists to fix --- the original failure in new clothes. Records are small (approximately 21{,}000 characters for 46 sessions of history), so completeness is affordable. The scaling path when it ceases to be affordable is a \emph{structured category scan} --- every member of a bucket, a cheap filter over small records --- not approximate retrieval.

\section{Memory-Quality Evaluation}
\label{sec:memquality}

\subsection{Setup}

We evaluate on \textbf{LongMemEval-S}~\cite{wu2024longmemeval}: 500 questions over conversational histories of roughly 115{,}000 tokens, spanning information extraction, multi-session reasoning, temporal reasoning, knowledge update, preference application, and abstention. Correctness is scored by an LLM judge using the benchmark's official \texttt{anscheck} prompt, ported verbatim rather than rewritten.

\textbf{The judge is held fixed at \texttt{gemma4:31b} in every cell}, so the reader is the only variable across model columns. Section~\ref{sec:discipline} reports what it cost to make that true rather than merely intended.

\subsection{Results}

\centering
\caption{LongMemEval-S, $n=500$. The oracle is handed the gold answer-bearing turns; the composite uses no gold annotations, only inputs available in production.}
\label{tab:lme_arms}
\resizebox{\columnwidth}{!}{
\begin{tabular}{lrrrr}
\toprule
\textbf{Arm} & \textbf{Correct} & \textbf{Acc.} & \textbf{Ctx.\ chars} & \textbf{Gen.\ s} \\
\midrule
composite @ \texttt{gemma4:31b} (v1 config) & 429 & 85.8\% & 26{,}056 & 0.85 \\
composite @ \texttt{gemma4:31b} (parity control) & 428 & 85.6\% & 25{,}822 & 0.93 \\
oracle-precision @ \texttt{gemma4:31b} & 419 & 83.8\% & 5{,}654 & 0.51 \\
\textbf{composite @ \texttt{glm-5.2}} & \textbf{448} & \textbf{89.6\%} & 25{,}822 & 4.17 \\
oracle-precision @ \texttt{glm-5.2} & 457 & 91.4\% & 5{,}654 & 0.78 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
}
\end{table}

Two figures for the same reader appear because a library moved underneath matching flags between runs; Section~\ref{sec:discipline} explains the control arm that separates them. \textbf{For cross-model claims the parity control's 428 is the correct figure}; 429 is the earlier configuration. The two differ by one question, so nothing rests on the choice, but they must not appear in one sentence without saying which arm each is.

Against its own gold-evidence ceiling the composite scores $+9$ on \texttt{gemma4} ($p = 0.39$) and $-9$ on \texttt{glm-5.2} ($p = 0.31$). \textbf{Both are failures to reject, not demonstrations of equivalence.} With discordant pairs in the eighties the interval comfortably admits a real difference of several questions, and an equivalence test would be required to claim parity. The defensible statement is that \emph{the consolidated layer reaches gold-evidence accuracy from production-available inputs, and no significant difference is detectable at $n=500$.}

\subsection{The Result That Does Not Require That Hedge}

Partitioning by the number of gold answer-bearing turns a question requires yields a sharper and strictly stronger claim.

\begin{table}[!htbp]
\centering
\caption{Accuracy by required evidence turns. The composite leads gold-evidence selection at one and two turns under \emph{both} readers.}
\label{tab:strata}
\resizebox{\columnwidth}{!}{
\begin{tabular}{lrrrr}
\toprule
\textbf{Answer turns} & \textbf{$n$} & \textbf{comp.\ @ glm} & \textbf{oracle @ glm} & \textbf{comp.\ @ gemma4} \\
\midrule
1 & 182 & \textbf{92.9\%} & 90.7\% & 91.2\% \\
2 & 229 & \textbf{93.0\%} & 91.7\% & 89.5\% \\
\textbf{3+} & \textbf{68} & \textbf{75.0\%} & \textbf{89.7\%} & \textbf{55.9\%} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
}
\end{table}

The one- and two-turn strata are \textbf{411 of 500 questions --- 82.2\% of the benchmark} --- and the composite leads on both, under both readers, while holding no gold annotations at all. Its \emph{entire} deficit is the 68 questions requiring three or more evidence turns: 51/68 against the oracle's 61/68, a gap of ten that accounts for the whole $-9$ net difference between the arms.

\begin{quote}
Consolidation is not losing evidence. It is losing multi-fact aggregation over evidence it holds.
\end{quote}

This also disposes of the obvious remedy. Retrieval depth was raised in a separate experiment: coverage of the known misses rose from 56.9\% to 94.4\% and a 17-of-25 cohort gain reproduced exactly --- yet the aggregate effect was $+3$ questions of 500, at $2.69\times$ context and $1.8\times$ latency, because deep retrieval improves findability and degrades aggregation. More context is what makes this stratum worse.

\section{Cross-Model Evaluation}
\label{sec:crossmodel}

\subsection{Reader Capability Is a Large Lever --- Once}

Swapping the reader from \texttt{gemma4:31b} to \texttt{glm-5.2}, judge held fixed, moves the composite $+20$ (McNemar $+32/-12$, $p = 0.0037$) and the gold-evidence ceiling $+38$ ($+49/-11$, $p = 7.6 \times 10^{-7}$). This is the largest effect measured anywhere in this work, and it is in the opposite direction to every read-path intervention we attempted.

The asymmetry is itself informative. \textbf{The stronger reader buys the oracle roughly twice what it buys the composite}, and the mechanism is structural: a record is a lossy summary fixed at write time, and a better reader cannot recover from it what was never written down, whereas raw turns retain everything a better reader might newly extract. \textbf{Consolidation caps the headroom a stronger reader can exploit.} The ratio's interval is wide, so this is reported as a direction, not a factor.

\subsection{But the Lever Saturates}

The natural extrapolation --- continue up the reader ladder --- does not hold. A second frontier-class reader, \texttt{deepseek-v4-pro}, evaluated on the development split at \textbf{byte-identical prompts} with the judge held fixed and recorded, scores \textbf{223/252 against \texttt{glm-5.2}'s 224}: net $-1$, $+6/-7$, $p = 1.000$, with only 13 of 252 pairs discordant. The two readers largely make the same decisions rather than trading errors.

\begin{table}[!htbp]
\centering
\caption{One rung of the reader ladder does not predict the next.}
\label{tab:saturation}
\resizebox{\columnwidth}{!}{
\begin{tabular}{lrr}
\toprule
\textbf{Reader swap} & \textbf{Net} & \textbf{$p$} \\
\midrule
\texttt{gemma4:31b} $\to$ \texttt{glm-5.2} (composite, $n=500$) & $+20$ & 0.0037 \\
\texttt{glm-5.2} $\to$ \texttt{deepseek-v4-pro} (composite, $n=252$) & $-1$ & 1.000 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
}
\end{table}

We therefore state a bounded conclusion. That a \emph{weak} reader binds is established. That \emph{further} reader capability is a lever is not, and one measurement says it is not. The scope is one additional reader on the development split; it refutes the extrapolation without establishing saturation as a general property.

\subsection{Latency Does Not Transfer}

At an identical 25{,}822-character prompt the frontier reader is $4.5\times$ slower at the median and $8\times$ at the mean (4.17\,s vs.\ 0.93\,s median; 9.21\,s vs.\ 1.15\,s mean). This was verified as a reader property rather than contention: latency is flat across run-order and prompt-size quintiles, the extraction leg was fully cached at 0.00\,s for all 500 questions, and generation is a single serial call in every arm. Notably, \texttt{deepseek-v4-pro} is $2.4\times$ \emph{faster} than \texttt{glm-5.2} at identical prompts while scoring the same, so latency and accuracy are not ordered together across readers.

\subsection{Judge Severity and Self-Judging}
\label{sec:judge}

Every figure here is graded by \texttt{gemma4:31b}, while published comparators are graded by frontier judges and the benchmark itself specifies GPT-4o. If a smaller judge grades more harshly, part of the reported gap would be judge severity rather than system quality. We attack this by \textbf{dispersion}: re-judging the committed \texttt{glm-5.2} arm's 500 hypotheses under three judges from unrelated model families, generation untouched.

\begin{table}[!htbp]
\centering
\caption{Judge panel over identical hypotheses. The self-judge cell is run deliberately.}
\label{tab:judges}
\resizebox{\columnwidth}{!}{
\begin{tabular}{lrrr}
\toprule
\textbf{Judge} & \textbf{Correct} & \textbf{Acc.} & \textbf{vs.\ incumbent} \\
\midrule
\texttt{gemma4:31b} (incumbent) & 448 & 89.6\% & --- \\
\texttt{deepseek-v4-pro} (third party) & 444 & 88.8\% & $+5/-9$ \\
\texttt{glm-5.2} (\emph{self-judge}) & 448 & 89.6\% & $+3/-3$ \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
}
\end{table}

Three judges agree on 97.0\% of questions (485/500 unanimous) and land within four of each other; the 15 contested questions split 9/5/9, so no judge is an outlier. \textbf{Two prior expectations failed, and both failures are recorded because they cut against convenient conclusions.}

First, the incumbent is \emph{not} a strict judge: the third-party judge scores this arm \textbf{lower}, 444 against 448. The confound runs opposite to the direction that would flatter this work and is bounded at roughly four questions. This closes it rather than merely bounding it.

Second, and more consequentially, \textbf{self-judging did not inflate the score}. The reader grading its own generations returns exactly the incumbent's 448 with symmetric flips. The standing argument against self-judged arms concerns \emph{verifiability}, and that argument stands; the stronger reading --- that self-judging materially inflates a result --- is not supported by the measurement available. We note the scope: one model, and a judge prompt that is a near-mechanical yes/no containment check, which is the setting offering a self-judge the least latitude. Self-preference would plausibly be stronger on open-ended quality judgements.

\section{Evaluation Discipline and Negative Results}
\label{sec:discipline}

We report this material as a contribution rather than an appendix. In an area where systems are compared across differing readers, judges, and metric definitions, the procedures that make a number mean something are as transferable as the number.

\subsection{Parity as an Enforced Invariant}

Two parity checks stood between the cross-model table and meaninglessness, and \textbf{one of them failed silently}.

\textbf{Judge parity.} The \texttt{-{}-judge-model} flag defaults to the reader, and result files recorded only the reader --- so a held-fixed judge was indistinguishable from a self-judge in the artefact, and a self-judged arm is comparable to nothing. Eighty hypotheses were re-judged under an explicit external judge, sampling \emph{all} of the arm's negative verdicts, where a self-judge would diverge: 80/80 agreement. Both harnesses now write the judge into result metadata.

\textbf{Configuration parity failed, and the flags could not show it.} Both composite arms logged identical flags, yet prompt lengths differed on 495 of 500 questions by a median of $-212$ characters. The cause was an unconditional call added to the renderer between runs --- \emph{no flag to log}. A library had moved underneath matching flags, and the composite-vs-composite contrast was therefore a reader swap plus two rendering changes.

The remedy generalises past the incident: a \texttt{-{}-assert-prompt-parity} gate takes a prior result file and aborts on the first prompt whose length differs, \emph{before} spending an LLM call on it. Parity becomes an enforced invariant of the artefact rather than a claim made about it. It was verified in both directions before use --- passing against one arm, aborting on question 1 against the other. \emph{A gate that never fires proves nothing.}

The control arm was then pre-registered with both branches fixed in advance, and landed at 428 ($-1$, $p = 1.000$): inside the band, both rendering changes null at scale. The contaminated contrast was $+19$; the clean one is $+20$. \textbf{The confound had deflated the effect rather than inflating it.}

\subsection{A Defect That Scored Silence as a Wrong Answer}

The frontier arm reported zero errors while containing four questions whose generated answer was the empty string. An empty generation carried no error marker, so it returned on the first pass, was judged incorrect, and was recorded as a substantive wrong answer. Only the long-context arm produced them, consistent with the visible answer being crowded out at long context.

Re-running those four under the fixed harness at byte-identical prompts, all four produce substantive answers and \textbf{one is correct}. We report this as \textbf{``448 as-scored, $+1$ repaired''}; 449 replaces 448 nowhere, because 448 is the artefact every contrast in this paper is computed against, and silently improving it after the fact would invalidate the control it is paired with.

\subsection{Six Reader-Side Interventions, Six Nulls}

\begin{table}[!htbp]
\centering
\caption{Every attempt to fix aggregation by changing what the reader is shown or told.}
\label{tab:nulls}
\resizebox{\columnwidth}{!}{
\begin{tabular}{llr}
\toprule
\textbf{Intervention} & \textbf{Kind} & \textbf{Effect} \\
\midrule
Co-referent collapse & rendering & $+1$, $p=1.000$ \\
Chronological \texttt{EVENT}/\texttt{UPDATE} order & rendering & $+1$, $p=1.000$ \\
Shipped system prompt & instruction & $-13$, $p=0.0044$ \\
Reconciliation hint & instruction & $-1$, $p=1.000$ \\
Premise guard & instruction & $-28$, $p=0.0018$ \\
Chronological \texttt{ITEM} order & rendering & $0/16$ cohort \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
}
\end{table}

The premise guard is the instructive failure. It did exactly what it was designed to do --- abstention rose from 22 to 30 of 30 --- and cost 28 questions overall, concentrated entirely in preference questions. Those are \emph{advice} questions graded on whether the response reflects the user's stated preferences; the records never contain the requested advice verbatim, so a literal premise check fires and the model refuses. The distinction the guard cannot draw is between ``the question asks for a fact the records do not contain'' and ``the question asks for advice the records inform.''

The final row was measured in this work. Category runs are grouped for counting, so \texttt{ITEM} records are never ordered chronologically; we hypothesised that this cost the temporal questions. Ordering \emph{within} each category run, with a control arm on the 16 real losses, converted \textbf{zero}, while the control converted one by pure nondeterminism at temperature zero. Both gates passed: control prompts were byte-identical to the committed arm, and the intervention genuinely fired (281 record lines changed position). \textbf{The reason is visible in the corpus: of 1{,}483 category runs, 1{,}310 (88\%) hold one or two entities.} The taxonomy is fine-grained enough that its categories are mostly singletons, so there is almost nothing for a within-category sort to sort.

\textbf{The control arm is the load-bearing part of that result.} Without it, ``the treatment converted one of sixteen'' would have been available, and wrong.

\subsection{A Fix Retired Before It Was Built}
\label{sec:killed}

The obvious response to a multi-fact aggregation deficit is a pre-aggregated cluster record written at consolidation time, whose cheap deterministic form is a per-category roster header. Before building it we read all seventeen losses individually and asked one question of each: \emph{would the header print the gold number?}

\begin{table}[!htbp]
\centering
\caption{What the 3+ stratum losses actually ask.}
\label{tab:shapes}
\resizebox{\columnwidth}{!}{
\begin{tabular}{llr}
\toprule
\textbf{Shape} & \textbf{Example} & \textbf{$n$} \\
\midrule
windowed & ``how many, \emph{in the past two weeks}'' & 5 \\
order & ``the \emph{order} of the three trips'' & 3 \\
predicate & ``projects I \emph{led}'' & 3 \\
argmax & ``which store did I spend the \emph{most} at'' & 2 \\
enumerate & plain category count & 3 \\
arithmetic & sum of stated quantities & 1 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
}
\end{table}

\textbf{Thirteen of seventeen apply a filter supplied by the question at read time.} A roster header would print the gold number on one, a wrong number on two, and would have no defined value on seven, where the target category fragments into runs of differing sizes. At most two conversions from a 51/68 baseline reaches 53 against a pre-registered bar of 58: \textbf{the intervention could not clear its own gate even at zero losses}, and was not built.

Two cases are active harm rather than nulls: on one question the header prints 3 where the model already answered 3 and gold is 4; on another it prints 4 where the model answered 4 and gold is 3. In both, a computed value would have \emph{confirmed} the wrong answer.

We also record two flattering readings removed from our own analysis, both of which moved the number unfavourably. Scoring convertibility as ``some run in the corpus has exactly the gold size'' yielded seven of seventeen and was coincidence matching --- on a baking question with gold 4 it matched an unrelated travel category of size 4. Scoring the largest matching run as ``printed'' then turned a fragmented case into a conversion when no single number would be printed at all.

\section{Comparison to Published Systems}
\label{sec:comparison}

Published LongMemEval results cluster at 94--96\%, against 89.6\% here. Before treating that as a capability gap we checked what each figure measures, because \textbf{the reported numbers are not all the same measurement}. Quotations below are verbatim from the publishing sources, accessed 2026-08-28.

\textbf{Metric definition differs.} Two leading figures are macro averages over question categories, not micro averages over questions. One system states that ``[o]verall accuracy is the unweighted average across all 6 categories''; another reports ``95.4\% (466/500)'', where the raw count is 93.2\%. Our headline, by contrast, is a micro average over all 500 questions with abstention included --- the strictest of the available definitions.

Recomputing our own arm under each comparator's metric:

\begin{table}[!htbp]
\centering
\caption{The same result under each metric definition. The headline is unchanged; these are labelled comparability figures.}
\label{tab:metrics}
\resizebox{\columnwidth}{!}{
\begin{tabular}{lrr}
\toprule
\textbf{Metric} & \textbf{This work} & \textbf{Comparator} \\
\midrule
raw micro, all 500 \emph{(headline)} & \textbf{89.6\%} & 93.2\% (raw) \\
macro over 5 categories & 90.9\% & 95.4\% \\
macro over 6 categories & 92.1\% & 94.87\% \\
raw micro, abstention excluded & 91.3\% & --- \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
}
\end{table}

The gap is real but roughly half what a naive column comparison implies: 2.8 points rather than 5.3 against one system's own metric, and 18 questions rather than 29 against another's raw count. \textbf{We do not adopt the friendlier figures.} Switching metrics after observing them is the manoeuvre this section identifies in others, and 89.6\% remains the reported result.

\textbf{Some comparators are not externally judged.} One system reports using a single model ``for both answering questions and judging correctness''; another names one model ``as the generation and grading LLM.'' We claim only that such figures are \emph{unverifiable} without an external check --- not that they are inflated. Section~\ref{sec:judge} is the reason for that restraint: we ran the self-judge configuration deliberately and it moved nothing.

\textbf{One widely-cited figure is not a QA score at all.} A 96.6\% result is retrieval recall at rank 5 --- whether the labelled session appears among the top five candidates. Its authors flag this prominently, warning that ``[r]etrieval recall and QA accuracy are not comparable; a system can have 100\% retrieval recall and 40\% QA accuracy, and vice versa.'' \textbf{An earlier draft of this work made exactly that error}, placing the figure in a column of QA accuracies; we record it as our misreading, not their misreporting.

\section{Localising the Residual}
\label{sec:residual}

Crossing the composite against the oracle under the same reader and judge partitions the residual into buckets implying different work. Abstention is held out, since its gold answer is a prose statement of non-answerability that can never appear in a record.

\begin{table}[!htbp]
\centering
\caption{Residual composition under \texttt{glm-5.2} (52 errors).}
\label{tab:residual}
\resizebox{\columnwidth}{!}{
\begin{tabular}{lrr}
\toprule
\textbf{Bucket} & \textbf{$n$} & \textbf{Share} \\
\midrule
benchmark/reader floor (oracle fails too) & 15 & 29\% \\
read-side: evidence present, unused & 16 & 31\% \\
write-side: evidence absent from records & 10 & 19\% \\
abstention calibration & 11 & 21\% \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
}
\end{table}

\textbf{The write-side bucket is approximately ten of 500 on both readers while every other bucket scales with reader capability}, and it is an upper bound twice over: the containment test counts paraphrase as absent, and reading all ten cases individually shows most are counting failures over evidence that is present. Only about three are true extraction loss. \textbf{Record extraction is close to saturated.}

\subsection{The Successor Problem}

Combining Section~\ref{sec:memquality}'s stratification with Section~\ref{sec:killed}'s shape analysis names the open problem precisely. It is not ``aggregation'' but \textbf{dynamic read-time filtered aggregation}: computing a count, an ordering, or an extremum over a subset selected by a predicate --- most often a relative date window --- that exists only in the question.

Every mechanism attempted here sits on the wrong side of that boundary. Write-time consolidation cannot see the predicate. Render-time totals cannot condition on it. Reader-side instruction and reordering have now returned six nulls at asking the model to do it unaided. And retrieval volume is not a lever: more context is what makes this stratum worse.

We state the ceiling arithmetic honestly. From 448, the aggregation bucket offers roughly ten questions --- now known not to be reachable by write-time clustering --- abstention offers at most eleven with the naive fix already measured at $-28$, and the empty-generation repair is closed at $+1$. \textbf{No lever identified in this work reaches 470.} Closing that distance is an open research question, and we believe it lives in mechanisms that condition on the question's predicate at read time, which no arrangement of a question-blind record block can provide.
